new_statements.quote: § 5. Die germanischen Akzentregeln haben auch in der Z. Ma. Geltung. Bei der Betonung des einzelnen Wortes ruht der Hauptakzent auf der Wurzelsilbe, gegen das Ende nimmt die Tonstärke und auch die Tonhöhe ab. [...] § 7. Der Starkton ruht wie im Mhd. bei einfachen Worten auf der Anfangssilbe: láilic Leintuch, mótɒ Mutter, táusət tausend. Fremdwörter behalten im allgemeinen ihren heimischen Akzent: afəkáat Advokat, apətéek Apotheke [...] Bei einigen Fremdwörtern, die den Ton auf der letzten oder vorletzten Silbe haben sollten, findet sich der Akzent auf der ersten Silbe: músic Musik, líkeeɒ Likör, [...] ékaal egal, khólenɒ Kalender.
new_statements.translation: S5. The Germanic accent rules also hold in the Zaisenhausen dialect. In the accentuation of the individual word the main accent rests on the root syllable; toward the end [of the word] the intensity and also the pitch decrease. [...] S7. As in MHG, in simple words the strong stress rests on the initial syllable: láilic 'Leintuch', mótɒ 'Mutter', táusət 'tausend'. Loanwords in general keep their native accent: afəkáat 'Advokat', apətéek 'Apotheke' [...] In some loanwords that ought to have the stress on the last or penultimate syllable, the accent is found on the first syllable: músic 'Musik', líkeeɒ 'Likör', [...] ékaal 'egal', khólenɒ 'Kalender'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Germanic root-syllable stress: primary stress falls on the root (stem) syllable, which in simple native words is the first syllable; intensity and pitch fall off toward the end of the word. Verbal prefixes are unstressed (stem stressed: fəsáufə 'ersaufen', phaltə 'behalten'), nominal prefixes are stressed (fóɒtl 'Vorteil', úunkheshtə 'Unkosten') except ge-. Loanwords mostly keep source (final/penult) stress, but a set of loans and personal names are shifted to initial stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Wanner S9 (p.267-268): in nominal compounds the first member carries the stress (súnəpluumə 'Sonnenblume'), also with genitival first members; S12: 'Volkssuperlative' (blütenweiß type) have both members almost equally stressed, in three-member forms the first two nearly equal and the third weak. Corroborated for core Southeast Palatine by Heeger 1896 S28 p.19 (file): 'In nominalen Zusammensetzungen ruht der Hauptton auf dem ersten Bestandteil, während der zweite den Nebenton trägt.'
new_statements.exceptions: Loans keep foreign accent (afəkáat, apətéek, khuráaš Courage, patról Patrouille), likewise native words with foreign suffixes (masióon 'Masse', kšteláaš 'Gestell'); some loans and names initial-stressed (músic, líkeeɒ, šílee gelée, pútl bouteille, ékaal, khólenɒ; márii Maria, ámarai Anna Maria, áatm Adam); vocatives always stress the first syllable (thétoor Theodor); prefix ge- unstressed in nouns; 'merkwürdig' final stress in mitdák 'Mittag', iwəráal 'überall'; place names stress the first member if the second is monosyllabic, otherwise the second (S10); double first names stress the first, name+trade combinations vary (S11).
new_statements.domain_note: Explicitly the word domain ('B. Der Wortton', 'Betonung des einzelnen Wortes'), distinguished from syllable accent (S6 'Silbenton': single-peaked) and from compound/name-group accent (SS9-12); examples are citation forms in the author's transcription with acute marking the stressed vowel.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement (Wanner 1907) describes the village dialect of Zaisenhausen (Kraichgau, north-east Baden, near Eppingen/Bretten). Glottolog 5.1 files this work under pala1330, but the forms in the article (apfl 'Apfel', pfefɒ 'Pfeffer', pfool 'Pfahl') place it south of the Speyer appel/apfel line, i.e. South Franconian (Suedrheinfraenkisch/Kraichgau), not core Pfaelzisch. The core-Palatine source opened (Heeger 1896, Suedostpfalz around Landau/Germersheim, Vorderpfalz) states only compound stress (first member) and presupposes the stem syllable as the 'starke Iktussilbe'. Khramova 2011 (Glottolog's 'grammar' for pala1330) describes Volga German of Milberger, Kansas, whose base dialect the author identifies as Hessian (Darmstadt area), and is silent on stress. Erdmann 1906 (Bingen) is Rheinhessisch; Boehmer 1909 is the Palatine speech island Pfalzdorf on the Lower Rhine.
